title: More than five senses: balance, body position, warmth, cold and pain

summary.text: A steel plate feels colder than a wooden board, even when both have sat in the same room all morning. Put an ice cube on each, and the ice on the steel melts first. Your skin does not read temperature like a thermometer. It feels how fast heat leaves it or comes into it. This is one of many senses that are not on the list of five. Your inner ears sense turning and tilting, your muscles tell you where your hands are, and pain warns you before you get badly hurt. Other animals have senses people lack: a fish feels the water move along their sides, and a prawn keeps their balance with grains of sand.
summary.art: A child's hand resting on a steel plate on one side and a wooden chopping board on the other, with an ice cube on each. The cube on the steel sits in a big puddle, and the cube on the wood is still almost whole.

intro.hook: Spin round slowly five times, then sit down. The room seems to keep turning, though you and the room are both still. What is still spinning?
intro.text: The answer is inside your ears. Deep in each ear are three tiny loops full of liquid. When you spin, the liquid starts to swirl. When you stop, it keeps swirling for a few seconds, so your brain thinks you are still turning. In this unit you find this sense and four more that are not on the list of five: the sense of where your body parts are, the sense of warmth and cold, the sense of pain, and the senses inside you. You test them with ice, steel plates, mint leaves and a bowl of water. Then you meet animals with senses people do not have.
intro.art: A girl sitting on a mat after spinning, holding her head, with the walls of the room drawn slightly tilted. A small cut-away picture shows three liquid-filled loops inside her ear.

outcomes: I can name at least four senses that are not on the list of five, and say what each one tells me.
I can explain why I feel dizzy after spinning, using the liquid in the loops of my inner ear.
I can explain why a steel plate feels colder than a wooden board at the same temperature, using my ice test as evidence.
I can say how my muscles and joints tell my brain where my hands and feet are, without my eyes.
I can explain how pain protects the body, and what happens to people who cannot feel it.
I can describe a sense that people lack but another animal has. I can say what problem the animal faces, and how the sense helps them live.
I can plan a fair test of a sense, say what I think will happen and why, and use what I saw to explain the result.

terms.meaning: A way your body detects something and tells your brain about it.
terms.example: Your balance sense tells you when you are tipping over, even with your eyes shut.
terms.art: A child standing on one foot with eyes shut, arms out, wobbling slightly.

terms.meaning: A special cell, or the end of a nerve, that detects one kind of thing, such as cold, stretch or a turn of the head.
terms.example: Cold receptors in your skin send a signal when your hand touches an ice cube.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of skin with tiny nerve endings under the surface, one of them lit up next to an ice cube.

terms.meaning: A long, thin bundle that carries signals between the brain and every part of the body.
terms.example: A nerve carries the signal from your fingertip to your brain when you touch a hot tumbler.
terms.art: An outline of a child's arm with a thin line running from the fingertip, up the arm, to the spine and brain.

terms.meaning: The sense that tells you which way is down, and when your head turns, tilts or speeds up. Its organs are deep inside each inner ear. Scientists call it the vestibular sense.
terms.example: Your balance sense tells you the lift has started to go up, even when the doors are shut.
terms.art: A girl in a lift with closed doors, her knees slightly bent, with a small picture of her inner ear beside her.

terms.meaning: Three tiny loops of tube in each inner ear, filled with liquid. When your head turns, the liquid lags behind and bends tiny hairs, and the hairs send signals to your brain.
terms.example: When you shake your head to say no, the liquid in one loop moves and tells your brain your head is turning.
terms.art: Three small curved loops joined together, at right angles to each other, coloured blue to show the liquid inside.

terms.meaning: Tiny crystals, made of the same stuff as chalk and seashells, that sit on a jelly over hair cells in your inner ear. Gravity pulls on them, so they tell you which way is down. Scientists call them otoliths.
terms.example: When you tilt your head to one side, the ear crystals slide a little and your brain knows you are tilted.
terms.art: A magnified drawing of a layer of jelly with tiny white crystals on top and hair cells poking up into it from below.

terms.meaning: The sense of where your body parts are and how they are moving. Stretch sensors in your muscles, tendons and joints tell the brain.
terms.example: You can scratch your ear in the dark because proprioception tells you where your hand is.
terms.art: A child in a dark room touching their own ear with one finger, with faint glowing lines in the arm muscles.

terms.meaning: The sense of warmth and cold. Separate receptors in the skin feel warming and cooling.
terms.example: When you step from a hot balcony into a room with the AC on, your skin feels the cold at once.
terms.art: A child stepping from a sunny balcony into a cool room, with small blue dots on the skin of the arms.

terms.meaning: A material that lets heat pass through it quickly. Metals are good conductors of heat. Wood, cloth and plastic are poor conductors.
terms.example: A steel spoon left in hot payasam gets hot all the way up its handle. A wooden ladle does not.
terms.art: A steel spoon and a wooden ladle standing in a pot of payasam, with red shading creeping up the steel spoon only.

terms.meaning: The sense that warns you something is damaging, or about to damage, your body. Pain receptors detect strong heat, cuts, crushing and harmful chemicals.
terms.example: A pinch from a tight chappal strap hurts, so you loosen it before it makes a blister.
terms.art: A child's foot in a chappal with a tight strap, a small red mark beside the strap.

terms.meaning: A quick movement your body makes without you choosing it, to protect you. The signal goes to your spinal cord and straight back to the muscle.
terms.example: Your hand jerks away from a hot vessel before you have time to think.
terms.art: A hand pulling back fast from a hot steel vessel on a stove, with motion lines.

terms.meaning: The senses inside your body. They tell you when you are hungry, thirsty, full, short of breath, or need the toilet.
terms.example: Your tummy rumbling and the empty feeling before lunch are interoception at work.
terms.art: A child holding their tummy and looking at a plate of idli on the table.

terms.meaning: A line of tiny sensors along each side of a fish's body. They feel the water moving around the fish.
terms.example: A rohu in a muddy pond feels a fish swimming close by through their lateral line, even when they cannot see it.
terms.art: A rohu fish seen from the side, with a thin dotted line running from the gills to the tail.

terms.meaning: A small balance pit in animals such as prawns, crabs and octopuses. Tiny grains or crystals rest on sensing hairs inside it, and show which way is down.
terms.example: A prawn has a statocyst at the base of each of their short feelers, holding grains of sand.
terms.art: A prawn, with a small circle drawn at the base of the short feelers and a zoomed-in picture of sand grains resting on hairs.

explanations.definition: A sense is a way the body detects something and tells the brain. Besides sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, people have a balance sense, a sense of body position, a temperature sense, a pain sense, and senses inside the body.
explanations.description: Each sense has its own receptors. Some sit where you can see them, like the eyes. Many are hidden. The balance organs are inside your head. The body-position sensors are inside your muscles and joints. Warm, cold and pain receptors are nerve endings in your skin and inside your body. Each kind of receptor turns what it detects into nerve signals. Your brain puts all the signals together. That is why you can walk down a dark staircase, feel that the bath water is too hot, and know when you are hungry.
examples: Walking down stairs in a power cut uses your balance sense and your body-position sense, because your eyes help very little.
Feeling that the tea in your tumbler is too hot to drink uses your temperature sense and your pain sense.
Knowing you need the toilet uses a sense inside your body.
explanations.art: A child going down a dark staircase holding the rail, with small labels: balance, body position, touch.
explanations.context: This card is about the senses that are not on the list of five, and where their receptors are.

explanations.concept: How your balance sense feels turning
explanations.definition: Each inner ear has three liquid-filled loops called semicircular canals. When the head turns, the liquid lags behind and bends tiny hairs, which send signals to the brain.
explanations.description: The three loops sit at right angles to each other, like the floor and two walls in the corner of a room. So one loop feels nodding, one feels shaking your head, and one feels tipping your head towards a shoulder. When you start to spin, the loops turn with your head, but the liquid inside is slow to start moving. It pushes against the hairs, and the brain knows you are turning. If you keep spinning, the liquid catches up and turns along with you. When you stop, the liquid keeps swirling for a few seconds. It bends the hairs the other way, and the brain thinks you are spinning in the opposite direction. That is dizziness. You saw the same thing with the bowl of water: the water kept turning after the bowl stopped.
examples: After a ride on a giant wheel at a temple festival, you may feel the ground sway for a moment.
Dancers who spin, such as Kathak dancers, fix their eyes on one spot and whip their head round, so they get less dizzy.
After spinning, a grown-up can see your eyes flick from side to side for a few seconds. The brain moves the eyes because it thinks the head is still turning.
explanations.art: Three linked loops of an inner ear beside a bowl of water still swirling after the bowl has stopped, with arrows on both.
explanations.context: This card explains why you feel dizzy after spinning, using the loops of liquid inside your ear.

explanations.concept: Ear crystals: which way is down
explanations.definition: Two small pouches in each inner ear hold tiny crystals of calcium carbonate on a layer of jelly. Gravity and speeding up make the crystals press or slide, and the hair cells below tell the brain.
explanations.description: Calcium carbonate is the same stuff as chalk and seashells. The crystals are heavier than the jelly around them. When you tilt your head, gravity pulls the crystals down a little, and they bend the hairs under them. When a lift starts to go up, the crystals lag behind for a moment and press down harder. So you feel the lift start, even with the doors shut. When it stops, you feel a moment of lightness. Your balance sense works only for changes. In a smooth lift moving at a steady speed, or a plane flying smoothly, you feel nothing at all.
examples: You feel the lift start and stop, but not the steady part of the ride.
Lying on your side, you still know which way is up with your eyes shut.
In space, there is no feeling of down, and many astronauts feel sick for the first few days.
explanations.art: A cut-away of a small pouch in the inner ear with crystals on a jelly layer, tilting to one side as a child tilts her head.
explanations.context: This card is about the tiny crystals in your ears that sense tilting, gravity and lifts.

explanations.definition: Proprioception is the sense of where your body parts are and how they move. Stretch sensors in muscles, and sensors in tendons and joints, send signals to the brain all the time.
explanations.description: Every muscle has tiny stretch sensors inside it. When your elbow bends, some muscles stretch and others get shorter, and the sensors report it. Sensors in your tendons feel how hard a muscle is pulling. Your brain puts these signals together into a picture of where each part of you is. That is how you can eat idli without looking at your hand, or type on a phone while looking at the screen. In the dot test, your pencil landed close to the dot with your eyes shut, but not exactly on it. Without your eyes to check, the body-position sense is good but not perfect.
examples: You can put a spoon of rice into your mouth while looking at the TV.
When your foot 'falls asleep' after sitting cross-legged, you cannot feel where it is, so it is hard to stand on.

In 2021, Ardem Patapoutian shared the Nobel Prize for finding Piezo2, a tiny gate in nerve endings that opens when they are stretched. People born without working Piezo2 have very poor body-position sense.
explanations.art: A child eating a dosa while looking up at a ceiling fan, with faint lines in the arm muscles leading to the brain.
explanations.context: This card explains the sense that tells you where your hands and feet are, without looking.

explanations.concept: Why steel feels colder than wood
explanations.definition: Your skin feels warmth and cold by how fast heat flows out of it or into it. Metals are good conductors of heat, so they draw heat from your skin quickly and feel colder.
explanations.description: Heat always flows from a warmer thing to a cooler thing. The skin of your hand is warmer than most rooms. Touch a steel plate, and the steel carries heat away from the skin very fast, so the skin cools quickly. Your cold receptors fire strongly, and you feel cold. Touch a wooden board at the same temperature, and the wood carries heat away slowly. The skin stays almost as warm, so the wood feels only a little cool. The ice test shows that it is not the plate itself that is colder. The ice was colder than both. Steel carried heat into the ice fast, so that cube melted first. Wood carried heat in slowly, so that cube lasted longer.
examples: The steel railing on a balcony feels colder than the wooden door in the morning, though both are at the temperature of the air.
A steel tumbler of tea feels hotter in your hand than a clay cup with the same tea, because steel carries heat into your skin fast.
A tiled floor feels colder to bare feet than a cotton mat on the same floor.
explanations.art: Two hands, one on a steel plate with arrows of heat rushing out of the palm, one on a wooden board with only a few slow arrows.
explanations.context: This card explains the Ice Race result: why steel feels colder, though ice melts faster on it.

explanations.definition: The skin has separate receptors for cold and for warmth. They are not spread evenly, and there are many more cold spots than warm spots.
explanations.description: In 1882, a Swedish scientist, Magnus Blix, touched the skin with a thin metal tip, point by point. Some points felt cold, some felt warm, and some felt only a touch. In 1884, Alfred Goldscheider in Germany found the same on his own. So warmth and cold are sensed by different receptors in different places. Cold receptors are the more common kind. That is why the cold-spot map on the back of your hand had cold squares and squares that felt only a touch. The same receptors can be fooled by chemicals. Menthol, in mint, switches on cold receptors, so your breath feels icy after a mint leaf. Capsaicin, in chilli, switches on heat receptors, so chilli feels hot. David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian shared the 2021 Nobel Prize for finding these receptors.
examples: After chewing pudina, a sip of room-temperature water feels cold.
Green chilli makes your mouth feel hot, though the chilli is no warmer than the rest of the food.
Some balms for aches contain menthol, and they feel cool on the skin.
explanations.art: The back of a hand with a small grid drawn on it, some squares marked with blue dots for cold and a few with red dots for warm.
explanations.context: This card is about the separate cold and warm receptors in your skin, and how mint and chilli fool them.

explanations.definition: Pain receptors detect things that damage the body: strong heat, deep cold, cuts, crushing and harmful chemicals. Pain makes you stop, pull away and look after the hurt part.
explanations.description: Pain is unpleasant on purpose. It makes you take your hand off the hot tawa, loosen a tight strap and rest a sprained ankle. Some protection is faster than feeling. When you touch something very hot, the signal goes to your spinal cord and straight back to your arm muscles. Your hand pulls away, often before you feel the pain. This is a reflex. A very small number of children are born unable to feel pain. They often get hurt without noticing: they bite their tongues, burn their hands and walk on broken bones. In the 1940s and 1950s, the surgeon Paul Brand found the same in people with leprosy in Vellore, as the how-we-found-out card tells. Pain is a gift that keeps the body whole.
examples: A small pebble in your shoe hurts, so you stop and shake it out before it makes a wound.
A sore throat makes you rest your voice.
Your hand jerks away from a hot vessel before you have even said 'ouch'.
explanations.art: A hand jerking back from a hot tawa, with a short arrow from the fingertip to the spine and straight back to the arm.
explanations.context: This card is about why we feel pain and how it protects us.

explanations.definition: Many animals have senses that people do not have. Each one helps that animal with a problem in their own life.
explanations.description: A fish in a muddy river cannot see far. They need to know where other fish and hunters are. Their lateral line, a row of sensors along each side, feels the water moving. So a shoal of sardines can turn together without bumping, even at night. A prawn lives in dark, moving water and must know which way is up. They keep grains of sand in a small pit at the base of each short feeler. When a prawn moults their shell, they lose the grains, and pick up new sand. A female mosquito needs blood to make her eggs, and must find someone in the dark. She senses the carbon dioxide in your breath from metres away, then your warmth and smell. A python hunts warm-bodied animals at night. Pits along their lips sense the heat from a rat's body. A spider's eyes see little, but the hairs and slits on their legs feel every shake of their web, so they know where an insect is caught.
examples: A shoal of mathi, sardines, off the Kerala coast turns all at once, using their lateral lines and eyes.
A mosquito finds you in a dark room by your breath and warmth.
A garden spider rushes to the exact spot where a fly hit the web.
explanations.art: Four small panels: a sardine with a dotted lateral line, a prawn with sand grains at the base of the feelers, a mosquito following a cloud of breath, a spider on a shaking web.
explanations.context: This card is about senses other animals have that people do not, and what each one is for.

explanations.concept: Why some people feel sick in a car or a boat
explanations.description: Many children feel sick reading in a moving car, or on a ferry. Nobody is completely sure why. The best-known idea is that the senses disagree. The ears feel the car turning and bumping. The eyes, looking at a book inside the car, see no movement at all. Another idea says the sickness comes from the body struggling to keep steady when the ground moves in an unfamiliar way. Both ideas agree on what helps: look out at the horizon, sit where the ride is smoothest, and get fresh air.
examples: Reading a book in a car on the ghat road to Ooty makes many children feel sick.
Looking out of the front window at the road often helps.
Sailors often stop feeling seasick after a few days at sea.

perspectives.who: Sensory conflict idea (James Reason and others, 1970s)
perspectives.explanation: The balance sense and the eyes send signals that do not match. The brain is confused by the mismatch, and the confusion makes you feel sick.

perspectives.who: Body-steadiness idea (Gary Riccio and Thomas Stoffregen, 1991)
perspectives.explanation: Sickness comes when the body cannot keep itself steady in a new kind of moving place. People who sway more before the trip are more likely to feel sick.

explanations.art: A child in the back seat of a car on a winding ghat road, looking pale over a book, while her mother points at the hills outside.
explanations.context: This card is about car sickness and sea sickness, which scientists still argue about.

explanations.description: Scientists do not agree on one number. It depends on how you count. If you count by kind of receptor, you find many: warmth, cold, pain, stretch, the three loops of the ear, the ear crystals, light, sound, the five basic tastes, many kinds of smell, and sensors that check your blood and your breath. If you count by experience, you get fewer. Some scientists say about 10, some say over 30.
examples: Is touch one sense, or several, since light touch, vibration, warmth, cold and pain each have their own receptors?
Is balance one sense, or two, since the loops feel turning and the crystals feel tilting?

perspectives.explanation: Each kind of receptor is a separate sense, because each detects something different. This gives more than 20.
Senses that feel alike, such as warmth and cold, are one sense. This gives about 10.

explanations.art: A child counting on her fingers in front of a chart with many small pictures: an ear, an eye, an ice cube, a flame, a stretched arm, a full glass of water.
explanations.context: This card is about a question with no single answer: how many senses we have.

agreed.text: People have many more than five senses, including balance, body position, warmth, cold, pain and senses inside the body.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have found a separate kind of receptor for each, and people who lose one of them, through illness or a rare gene, lose that sense only.

agreed.text: The semicircular canals in the inner ear sense the head turning, and the ear crystals sense tilting and speeding up.
agreed.evidence: In the 1820s, Pierre Flourens found that damaging the canals in pigeons upset their balance. Today doctors test the canals by watching the eyes after spinning or after warm or cool water is put in the ear.

agreed.text: The skin feels how fast heat flows in or out of it, so good conductors of heat feel colder or hotter than poor conductors at the same temperature.
agreed.evidence: A thermometer shows a steel plate and a wooden board in the same room are at the same temperature. Yet ice melts faster on the steel, and the steel feels colder.

agreed.text: Pain protects the body, and people who cannot feel pain get injured far more often.
agreed.evidence: Doctors have followed children born unable to feel pain, and people with leprosy whose nerves were damaged. Both get burns, cuts and broken bones without noticing.

agreed.text: Fish feel water movement through their lateral line, and prawns and crabs sense which way is down using grains in a balance pit.
agreed.evidence: Fish with a blocked lateral line swim less well in a shoal. In 1893, Alois Kreidl gave freshly moulted shrimps iron filings instead of sand, and the shrimps tilted when he held a magnet near them.

challenging.who: Aristotle, about 2,350 years ago, and many school books since
challenging.for: Five senses each have an organ you can point to, so the list is easy to teach.
challenging.against: Balance, body position, warmth, cold and pain each have their own receptors. Anyone can test them, as you did with the bowl, the dot and the ice.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that there are only five senses.

challenging.who: A very common idea, because metal feels colder
challenging.for: When you touch them, the steel really does feel colder than the wood.
challenging.against: Left in the same room, both reach the same temperature, as a thermometer shows. Ice melts faster on the steel, which could not happen if the steel were colder.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that metal things are colder than other things in the same room.

challenging.claim: Pain is bad, and life would be better without it.
challenging.who: Many people, when they are hurting
challenging.for: Pain is unpleasant, and long-lasting pain from an illness can make life very hard.
challenging.against: People who cannot feel pain get badly hurt without knowing. Short, sharp pain is a warning that protects the body. Long-lasting pain is different and needs a doctor's help.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that we would be better off without pain.

challenging.claim: Feeling dizzy means something is wrong with you.
challenging.who: Some children, the first time they get dizzy
challenging.for: Dizziness feels strange and can make you fall.
challenging.against: Dizziness after spinning is your balance sense working correctly: the liquid in the loops keeps moving after you stop. Dizziness that comes for no reason, again and again, should be checked by a doctor.
challenging.context: This card is about whether dizziness after spinning is a problem.

big_questions.q: Your skin said the steel was colder, but the ice said it was not. When a sense and a test disagree, which one tells you the truth?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one really measured: the heat leaving your hand, or the temperature of the plate.

big_questions.q: When you stop spinning, the room seems to turn. Where is that turning: in the room, in your ears, or in your mind?
big_questions.hint: Think about the liquid that keeps swirling in the loops, and what your brain does with the signal.

big_questions.q: A prawn feels which way is down using sand grains they picked up. Is the sand part of the prawn?
big_questions.hint: The sand came from the sea floor, and it does a job inside the prawn's body.

big_questions.q: A fish feels the water move, and a mosquito senses your breath. What might be all around us that no person can sense?
big_questions.hint: Think of all the senses people lack, and what each one picks up.

big_questions.q: Pain hurts, but it keeps us safe. Can something unpleasant also be a kind of care?
big_questions.hint: Think about the children and adults who could not feel pain, and what happened to their hands and feet.

big_questions.q: You feel your hand even with your eyes shut. How do you know a hand is yours?
big_questions.hint: Think about the stretch sensors in your muscles and the signals they send all the time.

story.title: The Prawn Who Picked Up Sand
story.note: The story is made up, and the people in it are not real. The science is true: prawns and shrimps keep sand grains in a balance pit at the base of their short feelers, lose them when they moult and pick up new ones. Alois Kreidl's iron filings test was done in Austria in 1893. Looking at the horizon helps many people with seasickness, though not everyone.
text: The ferry from Ernakulam to Vypin was crowded and loud. Arjun was eight, and he had been looking forward to this trip all week. His aunt, Reshma Chechi, studied prawns at a laboratory on the island. Today she was taking him to see them.
But the ferry rocked. Arjun had brought his comic, and he was reading it on the bench. After a few pages his tummy began to feel strange. His mouth filled with spit. His forehead was cold and damp.
"Chechi," he said, "I think I'm going to be sick."
Reshma Chechi took the comic gently out of his hands. "Look out there," she said, and pointed at the line where the grey water met the sky. "Keep your eyes on that line. Breathe slowly."
Arjun looked. The ferry went up and down, and the far line stayed still. Slowly, his tummy settled.
"Why did that help?" he asked.

"Inside your ears you have balance organs," his aunt said. "They felt the boat rocking. But your eyes were on the comic, which was rocking with you. So your eyes said 'nothing is moving', and your ears said 'everything is moving'. Many scientists think that kind of disagreement is what makes people feel sick. When you looked at the horizon, your eyes saw the rocking too. Your eyes and ears agreed again."
At the lab there were long rows of glass tanks, bubbling softly. Reshma Chechi led him to one with sand at the bottom. Small, see-through prawns hung in the water, their long feelers waving.
"Look at that one," she said. In the corner of the tank lay something that looked like a whole prawn, but empty and thin as paper.
"Is it dead?" Arjun whispered.

"That is a shell," she said. "A prawn's shell does not grow. So when a prawn gets too big, they wriggle out of the old shell and grow a new one. This is called moulting. The prawn who left that shell is over there, soft and new."
She pointed at a prawn near the sand. The prawn was tilting oddly, leaning to one side, then the other.
"Why is she wobbling?" asked Arjun.

"Because she has lost her balance stones," said his aunt. "At the base of a prawn's short feelers there is a tiny pit. Inside it are hairs, and on the hairs sit a few grains of sand. When the prawn tips, the grains roll and press on the hairs. That tells her which way is down. But the pit is part of the shell. When she moulted, the old pit went away with the old shell, sand and all."
"So how does she get new ones?"
"Watch."
The prawn dipped her head to the sand. Her tiny front legs moved quickly, picking at the grains. A few minutes later she was swimming straight and steady.
Arjun's mouth fell open. "She put sand in her own head!"

Reshma Chechi laughed. "More or less. In 1893, a scientist in Austria called Alois Kreidl had a clever idea. He put freshly moulted shrimps in a tank with no sand at all, only tiny bits of iron, called iron filings. The shrimps picked up the iron and put it in their balance pits. Then Kreidl held a magnet above them."
"What happened?"
"The magnet attracted the iron towards it. So the shrimps felt as if down had moved. They tipped over to one side, as if the sea floor had moved."
Arjun laughed out loud. Then he stopped. "Chechi, I don't have sand in my ears. Do I?"

"Not sand," said his aunt. "But very close. In each of your inner ears there are two little pouches. They hold thousands of tiny crystals, made of the same stuff as chalk and seashells. They rest on a jelly, on top of hairs. When you tilt your head, the crystals slide a little, and the hairs tell your brain. Your body made those crystals itself. The prawn borrows hers from the sea floor."
"And the rocking on the ferry?"
"That is a different part. You also have three tiny loops full of liquid in each ear. They feel your head turning, and the boat kept turning you this way and that."
On the ferry home, the sun was low and orange. The ferry rocked just as much as before. Arjun did not open his comic. He sat at the rail and kept his eyes on the line where the water met the sky.
He tilted his head slowly to one side, and then to the other. He imagined thousands of tiny crystals sliding on their jelly, and the hairs underneath sending their signals.
"Chechi," he said, "the prawn and I are doing the same thing."
"Yes," said Reshma Chechi. "With different stones."
story.epiphany: For the parent: balance comes from something heavy resting on sensing hairs. When the head tips, gravity pulls the heavy bits, they press on the hairs, and the brain knows which way is down. A prawn uses grains of sand. People use tiny crystals of calcium carbonate made by the body. Seasickness is not fully understood, but the best-known idea is that the eyes and the balance sense disagree, and looking at the horizon helps them agree.
ask: Why did Arjun feel sick while reading his comic on the ferry?
Why did the prawn wobble after she moulted?
What did the shrimps do when Alois Kreidl held a magnet above them? Why?
What is in your own ears that does the same job as the prawn's sand?
Arjun said he and the prawn were doing the same thing. Do you agree? What is the same, and what is different?

experiments.title: The Ice Race: does ice melt slower on the colder-feeling plate?
experiments.question: A steel plate feels colder than a wooden board. If we put an ice cube on each, which one melts first?
experiments.predict: Touch the steel plate and the wooden board. Which feels colder? Now guess: on which one will the ice cube melt first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Leave both surfaces in the same room for at least an hour, out of the sun and away from the fan, so they reach the same temperature. Use two ice cubes of the same size from the same tray. Put them down at the same moment. Only the surface changes.
results_table: How it felt to my hand
My guess: melts first or last?

materials.item: a steel plate, such as a thali, or a steel vessel lid
a wooden chopping board. No wooden board? Use a plastic chopping board or a thick hardback book in a plastic bag.
2 ice cubes of the same size, from the same ice tray in the freezer
a clock or phone that shows minutes
a cloth to wipe up
an aluminium vessel or lid, if you have one, for a third cube

experiments.safety: No heat is used. Wipe up melted water so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Touch the steel and the wood, guess, then race two ice cubes and check every 5 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the two cubes as they looked after 10 minutes, with their puddles.

flow.do: 1. An hour before, put the steel plate and the wooden board side by side on a table. 2. Keep them out of the sun and away from the fan. 3. Now your child presses one palm flat on each for 5 seconds.
flow.say: These two have been sitting in the same room for an hour. Put one hand flat on each. Which one feels colder?
flow.kid: Put one hand on the steel. Put the other hand on the wood. Which feels colder?

ask.q: Which one feels colder? Is it really colder, do you think?
good: I am not sure, they have been in the same room.

flow.parent: Almost everyone says the steel feels colder. Accept whatever your child says about why. Do not explain yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ice Race. You compare how a steel plate and a wooden board feel, then race ice cubes on them.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both in the table.
flow.say: Now we will put an ice cube on each. On which one will the ice melt first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: An ice cube goes on each. Which one melts first? Why?
flow.parent: Many children say the ice will last longer on the steel, because the steel feels colder. That is a good guess with a good reason. Let the test answer it.

flow.do: 1. Take two ice cubes from the same tray. 2. Put one in the middle of the plate and one in the middle of the board, at the same moment. 3. Look every 5 minutes. 4. Write what you see each time.
flow.say: Both cubes go down together. Now we watch. Every 5 minutes, tell me how big each cube is and how big its puddle is.
flow.kid: Put both cubes down at the same time. Look every 5 minutes. Which cube is getting smaller faster?
flow.parent: The cube on the steel melts much faster. In a warm room it is often a puddle in 10 to 15 minutes, while the cube on the wood is still mostly whole. Steel thalis are thin, so the difference is smaller than with a thick metal. If the difference is small, add a third cube on an aluminium vessel or lid. Aluminium carries heat even faster than steel. While you wait, you can play a round of Which Sense Told You?, but do not explain the result yet.

check.q: The ice on the steel plate melted first. The steel had felt colder. What does this tell you?
options: The steel was not really colder than the wood
The ice on the wood was a bigger cube
check.why: If the steel were colder, its ice would last longer. Both sat in the same room, so both were at the same temperature. The steel melted the ice faster because it carries heat quickly from the room into the ice. Picking 'a bigger cube' is fair to check, so swap the cubes next time. Steel makes no heat of its own.

flow.do: Touch the steel plate where the ice was, and the wooden board where its ice was.
flow.say: Touch the steel under the puddle. Now touch the wood under its cube. What do you feel now?
flow.kid: Touch the steel under the puddle. Touch the wood under its cube. What do you feel?
flow.parent: The steel feels icy all around the puddle, because it gave its heat to the ice. The wood is cold only right under the cube. Heat moves through steel quickly, and through wood slowly.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A strong answer: What I think: the steel was not colder than the wood, it only felt colder. What I saw: the ice melted faster on the steel. Why: steel carries heat fast. It takes heat out of my hand fast, so it feels cold. It gives heat to the ice fast, so the ice melts. My skin feels heat leaving, not the temperature.

check.q: Why did the steel feel colder to your hand?
options: It was at a lower temperature than the wood
It carried heat away from your hand faster
check.why: The steel carried heat away from your warm skin fast, so your skin cooled quickly and your cold receptors fired. The ice test shows it was not at a lower temperature. A steel plate left in the sun feels hot, so steel is not always cold.

experiments.context: In this experiment you race two ice cubes, one on a steel plate and one on a wooden board, to find out what your sense of cold really feels.

experiments.title: Find the Dot: how well do your hands know where they are?
experiments.question: With your eyes shut, how close can your pencil come to a dot you have just seen? Is your writing hand better than your other hand?
experiments.predict: Will your pencil land on the dot with your eyes shut? Will your writing hand do better than your other hand? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same dot, the same chair and the same starting place each time. Rest your hand in your lap before every try. Do 5 tries with each hand, because one try can be luck. Measure every miss with a ruler.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with a dot drawn in the middle with a sketch pen, as big as a one-rupee coin
a pencil
a ruler with centimetres
a cloth or dupatta to cover the eyes, if your child likes

experiments.safety: Use a blunt pencil. Keep the other hand away from the paper.

schedule.what: Look at a dot, shut your eyes, and try to touch it with a pencil. Measure the misses for each hand.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Circle your smallest miss. Write the total miss for each hand.

flow.do: 1. Tape the paper to a table. 2. Your child sits facing it, with the pencil in their writing hand, resting in their lap. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: You will look at the dot, shut your eyes, and try to touch it with your pencil. Will you hit it? Which hand will do better? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the dot. Then shut your eyes. Can you touch it? Which hand will do better? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Dot. You test the sense that tells you where your hand is, without your eyes.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks at the dot for 3 seconds, then shuts their eyes. 2. They lift the pencil from their lap and touch the paper once. 3. Mark the spot with a number. 4. Back to the lap. Do 5 tries.
flow.say: Look at the dot. Now eyes shut. Lift your pencil and touch the paper once. Back in your lap. Again.
flow.kid: Look. Shut your eyes. Touch the paper once. Hand back in your lap. Do it 5 times.
flow.parent: Do not say how close they are until all 5 tries are done, or they will correct their aim.

flow.do: Turn the paper over and do 5 tries with the other hand. Then measure each miss with a ruler, from the middle of the dot to the pencil mark.
flow.say: Now the other hand, 5 times. Then we will measure how far each mark is from the dot.
flow.kid: Now use your other hand, 5 times. Then measure each miss with the ruler.
flow.parent: Most children land within 1 to 4 centimetres of the dot. The writing hand is often a little closer, but not always. Some children find no difference.

flow.do: Add up the misses for each hand. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Your eyes were shut, but your pencil still came close. How did your hand know where to go? What did you see, and why did it happen?
flow.kid: Your eyes were shut. How did your hand know where to go?

ask.q: How did your hand get close to the dot without your eyes?
good: My arm knows where it is.
Stretch sensors in my muscles told my brain where my hand was.
I remembered where the dot was, and my body sense moved my hand there.

flow.parent: A strong answer: my pencil landed about 2 centimetres from the dot, so my body knows where my hand is even without my eyes. The sense is called proprioception. Stretch sensors in my muscles and joints told my brain. It was not perfect, because my eyes usually help to check.

check.q: With eyes shut, Meena's pencil landed 2 centimetres from the dot. What does this show?
options: Her body can sense where her hand is without her eyes, but not perfectly
check.why: Stretch sensors in her muscles and joints tell her brain where her hand is. That gets her close. Her eyes usually make the last small correction, so with them shut she misses by a little. If she had peeked, she would have hit the dot.

experiments.context: In this experiment you test the sense that tells you where your hand is, by touching a dot with your eyes shut.

experiments.title: The Dizzy Timer: does more spinning mean longer dizziness?
experiments.question: If you spin 10 times instead of 5, does the dizzy feeling last longer?
experiments.predict: Will the dizziness after 10 turns last longer than after 5 turns, the same, or shorter? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Spin at the same speed each time, about one turn every 2 seconds, in the same direction. Sit down straight after. Rest 3 minutes between tries, until you feel completely normal. Time each try the same way.
results_table: Seconds until the room stops spinning
Did the eyes flick? For how many seconds?

materials.item: a clear space on the floor, with a mat or carpet, away from furniture
a chair or the floor to sit on
a phone with a stopwatch

experiments.safety: A grown-up stands close the whole time. Spin slowly, on a mat, away from furniture and stairs. Sit down straight after spinning. Stop at once if your child feels sick. Children who get headaches or feel sick easily should only watch, or time a grown-up instead.

schedule.what: Spin 5 times, then 10 times, and time how long the dizzy feeling lasts each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw two bars, one for 5 turns and one for 10.

flow.do: Clear a space and put down a mat. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: You will spin 5 times, sit down, and tell me when the room stops spinning. Then you will try 10 times. Which will last longer? Why?
flow.kid: You will spin 5 times, then 10 times. Which dizziness lasts longer? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dizzy Timer. You time how long dizziness lasts after spinning 5 and 10 times.

flow.do: 1. Your child spins slowly 5 times, with arms out. 2. They sit down at once. 3. Start the stopwatch. 4. Look at their eyes. 5. Stop the watch when they say the room is still.
flow.say: Spin slowly, 5 times. Now sit. Look straight at my face. Say 'stop' when the room stops moving.
flow.kid: Spin slowly 5 times. Sit down. Look at a grown-up's face. Say stop when the room is still.
flow.parent: Watch your child's eyes closely. For a few seconds they flick from side to side by themselves. The brain moves the eyes because it thinks the head is still turning. Write down how long the flicking lasts too.

flow.do: Rest 3 minutes. Then do the same with 10 turns, at the same speed.
flow.say: Rest until you feel normal. Now 10 turns, the same speed. Sit, look at my face, and say 'stop' when it is over.
flow.kid: Rest first. Now spin 10 times, same speed. Sit. Say stop when the room is still.
flow.parent: Most children feel dizzy for longer after 10 turns, often a few seconds to 20 seconds. Turning longer gets the liquid in the ear loops moving faster, so it takes longer to stop. Every body is different, so results vary.

flow.do: Compare the two times. Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Which time was longer? What do you think is still moving after you stop?
flow.kid: Which dizziness lasted longer? What keeps moving after you stop?
flow.parent: A strong answer: after 10 turns, the dizziness lasted longer. The liquid in the loops of my inner ear was swirling more, so it took longer to stop. While it was still swirling, my brain thought I was turning.

check.q: Why does the room seem to spin after you stop?
options: The room really moves a little
The liquid in your ear loops keeps swirling for a few seconds
check.why: The liquid in your semicircular canals keeps moving after your head stops. It bends the tiny hairs, so your brain thinks you are still turning. The room does not move, and your eyes are fine. They flick because the brain thinks the head is turning.

experiments.context: In this experiment you time how long dizziness lasts after spinning, to see what your balance sense does.

activities.title: Spin and Stop: the water that keeps turning

materials.item: a round steel bowl or vessel, half full of water
a small piece of paper, as big as a fingernail, with an arrow drawn on it
a steel plate to stand the bowl on, so it turns easily
a mat on the floor

activities.safety: Spin slowly on a mat, away from furniture, with a grown-up close. Sit down straight after spinning.

schedule.what: Spin and feel the dizziness. Then turn a bowl of water and watch the water keep turning after the bowl stops.

activities.record: Draw the bowl with the paper arrow: once while you turn the bowl, and once after it stops.

flow.do: Your child spins slowly 5 times on the mat, then sits down.
flow.say: Spin slowly 5 times, then sit down. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Spin slowly 5 times. Sit down. What do you notice?

ask.q: What did you notice when you sat down?
good: I felt like I was still spinning.

flow.context: This is the first step of Spin and Stop. You feel dizziness, then make a model of what happens inside your ears.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bowl of water on the steel plate. 2. Float the paper arrow in the middle. 3. Wait until the water is still. 4. Quickly turn the plate a quarter turn. Watch the arrow.
flow.say: I will turn the bowl quickly, a little bit. Watch the arrow. Does the water turn with the bowl?
flow.kid: Watch the paper arrow. The bowl turns. Does the arrow turn too?
flow.parent: The bowl turns, but the water and the arrow hardly move at first. Water is slow to start moving. The liquid in the loops of the inner ear lags behind in the same way when your head starts to turn. That lag bends tiny hairs, and the brain knows you are turning.

flow.do: 1. Now turn the plate round and round, steadily, for 20 seconds. 2. Then stop the bowl suddenly and hold it still. 3. Watch the arrow.
flow.say: Now I keep turning the bowl for a while. Then I stop it. Watch the arrow when I stop.
flow.kid: The bowl turns and turns, then stops. What does the arrow do?
flow.parent: After 20 seconds the water turns along with the bowl. When the bowl stops, the water keeps swirling for several seconds. This is what happens in your ears after you stop spinning, and it is why the room seems to keep turning.

check.q: The bowl stopped, but the water kept turning. What in your body is like that water?
options: The liquid in the loops of your inner ear
check.why: The semicircular canals in your inner ear are loops of liquid. After you stop spinning, the liquid keeps swirling for a few seconds, just like the water in the bowl. So your brain thinks you are still spinning.

flow.do: Talk about what the model shows.
flow.say: Your head is like the bowl, and the liquid in your ear is like the water. When you stopped spinning, what was still turning?
flow.kid: Your head is the bowl. The liquid in your ear is the water. What kept turning?
flow.parent: A good answer: my head stopped, but the liquid in my ears kept swirling, so my brain thought I was still spinning.

activities.context: In this activity you spin to feel dizziness, then turn a bowl of water to see why it happens.

activities.title: The Floating Arm and the Thumb Hunt

materials.item: a doorway
a clock or phone with seconds

activities.safety: Press gently, not with full strength. Stand away from the door hinge.

schedule.what: Make your arm float up on its own, then find your thumb with your eyes shut.

activities.record: Write how high your arm floated. Write how many times out of 5 you found your thumb first time.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands in a doorway with arms straight down. 2. They press the backs of both hands outwards against the door frame, firmly, for 30 seconds. 3. Then they step forward out of the doorway and let their arms relax.
flow.say: Press the backs of your hands out against the door frame. Keep pressing while I count to 30. Now step forward and let your arms go loose. What happens?
flow.kid: Press your hands out on the door frame. Count to 30. Step out and relax. Watch your arms!
flow.parent: For most people, the arms float up by themselves, as if they were light. This is called the Kohnstamm effect. The muscles keep working for a short time after you stop pressing. Your body-position sense tells you the arms are rising, though you did not decide to lift them. Scientists still study exactly why it happens. If nothing happens, try pressing a little harder for 45 seconds.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Floating Arm. You make your arm rise on its own, then test how well you know where your hands are.

flow.do: 1. Your child shuts their eyes. 2. Gently move their left arm to a new place in the air and leave it there. 3. They touch their left thumb with their right pointing finger, in one go. 4. Do 5 different places.
flow.say: Eyes shut. I will move your left hand somewhere. Now find your left thumb with your right finger, in one go.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. A grown-up moves your left hand. Find your left thumb with one finger.

ask.q: You could not see your left hand. How did your finger find the thumb?
good: My arm knew where it was.
The muscles in my arm told my brain.
I could feel where my hand was.

flow.parent: Most children find the thumb almost every time. The stretch sensors in the muscles of the moved arm told the brain where the hand was. This sense is called proprioception.

activities.context: In this activity you feel your body-position sense at work in two ways.

activities.title: Cool Breath: mint fools your cold sense

materials.item: 2 or 3 fresh pudina, mint, leaves. Or a mint sweet, or a small dab of mint toothpaste.
a glass of water from the tap, at room temperature

activities.safety: Wash the leaves first. Toothpaste is for tasting a tiny dab only, not for swallowing.

schedule.what: Chew mint, breathe in through your mouth, and sip water. Notice how cold it feels.

activities.record: Write how the air and the water felt before and after the mint.

flow.do: Your child takes a deep breath in through the mouth and a sip of water. Ask how cold each feels, from 1 to 5.
flow.say: Breathe in through your mouth. Now take a sip. How cold is each, from 1 to 5?
flow.kid: Breathe in through your mouth. Sip the water. How cold, from 1 to 5?
flow.context: This is the first step of Cool Breath. You test whether mint can make your mouth feel cold.

flow.do: 1. Your child chews the mint leaves for 30 seconds and spits them out. 2. They breathe in through the mouth again. 3. Then they take another sip.
flow.say: Chew the mint for 30 seconds. Now breathe in through your mouth. Now sip. How cold now, from 1 to 5?
flow.kid: Chew the mint. Breathe in. Sip the water. How cold now?
flow.parent: The air and the water feel much colder, though nothing has changed temperature. Mint contains menthol. Menthol switches on the cold receptors in your mouth, the same ones that fire when something cold touches you.

flow.do: Talk about what this shows.
flow.say: The water came from the same glass. Was it really colder after the mint? What changed?
flow.kid: The water was the same. Was it really colder? What changed?

check.q: After chewing mint, the same water felt colder. Why?
options: Menthol in mint switches on your cold receptors

activities.title: Cold Spot Map: is all your skin the same?

materials.item: a washable sketch pen
a steel key, or the end of a steel spoon handle
a cup of ice water
a dry cloth
a sheet of paper with a 4 by 4 grid drawn on it, for the results

activities.safety: The key is only cold, never hot. Touch lightly.

schedule.what: Draw a grid on the back of your hand. Touch each square with a cold key and mark where it feels cold.

activities.record: On the paper grid, colour each square blue if it felt cold and leave it white if it felt only like a touch.

flow.do: Draw a small grid of 16 squares on the back of your child's hand, each square about as wide as a pencil.
flow.say: I am drawing a grid on your hand. We will test each square with a cold key. Will every square feel cold? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grid goes on your hand. Will every square feel cold? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cold Spot Map. You test whether every bit of your skin feels cold the same.

flow.do: 1. Dip the tip of the key in the ice water for 10 seconds. 2. Wipe it dry. 3. Your child shuts their eyes. 4. Touch the tip lightly in the middle of one square. 5. They say 'cold' or 'just touch'. 6. Mark it on the paper. Re-cool the key every 3 squares.
flow.say: Eyes shut. I will touch you with the key. Tell me: cold, or just touch?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Say cold or just touch each time.
flow.parent: Some squares feel clearly cold, and some feel only like a touch. Cold receptors are spread in small spots, with gaps between. If every square feels cold, use a thinner tip, such as the end of an opened steel paper clip, and smaller squares. In 1882, Magnus Blix mapped cold and warm spots in the same way.

flow.do: Look at the map together.
flow.say: Look at your map. Is your skin the same everywhere?
flow.kid: Look at your map. Where are your cold spots?
flow.parent: A good answer: no, some spots feel cold and others do not. My skin has cold receptors in some places and not in others.

activities.context: In this activity you map the cold spots on your skin, the way a scientist did in 1882.

activities.title: Feel Like a Fish: sensing water move

materials.item: a big bucket or basin, half full of water
a steel spoon
a towel

activities.safety: Do it on a floor that can get wet, such as the bathroom. Wipe up spills.

schedule.what: With eyes shut, feel the water move against your hand and point to where it came from.

activities.record: Write how many times out of 6 you pointed to the right side.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts one hand flat in the middle of the water, eyes shut, and keeps very still. 2. Wait until the water is still. 3. Move the spoon quickly, on one side of the hand, about 10 cm away, without touching. 4. They point to where the movement came from. 5. Do 6 tries, on different sides.
flow.say: Keep your hand still in the water, eyes shut. When you feel the water move, point to where it came from.
flow.kid: Hand still in the water. Eyes shut. Feel the water move? Point to where it came from.
flow.parent: Most children feel the water push against their hand and point to the right side most times. A fish has a lateral line, a row of sensors along each side, that does this much better. It helps them feel a hunter coming or a shoal turning, even in muddy water.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel Like a Fish. You try the sense fish use to feel water move.

flow.do: Talk about why a fish needs this sense.
flow.say: A fish in a muddy river cannot see far. Why would feeling the water move help them?
flow.kid: A fish cannot see far in muddy water. How does feeling the water help?

ask.q: How does feeling the water move help a fish?
good: They can feel a big fish coming to eat them.
They can swim with the other fish without bumping.
They can find food that is moving.

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: If something hurts a lot, or for a long time, tell a grown-up at once.

schedule.what: Start the diary. Write every message your hidden senses gave you today.
Count the messages for each sense and talk about what they did for you.

projects.record: A table with five columns: balance, body position, warm and cold, pain, and inside senses. Under each, write the message and what you did about it.

flow.do: Rule five columns in the notebook: balance, body position, warm and cold, pain, inside senses. Talk about one example for each.
flow.say: For five days we will catch the messages your hidden senses send you. Feeling hungry is one. A pebble in your chappal is another. What happened today?
flow.kid: Make five columns. Write each message your body sent you today.

flow.say: Which sense sent you the most messages? Which message kept you safe?
flow.kid: Count each column. Which sense spoke most? Which one kept you safe?

challenges.title: Guard the Feet: help someone who cannot feel pain in their feet
challenges.problem: Some people cannot feel pain in their feet. This can happen with leprosy, or after many years of the illness diabetes. They do not notice a sharp stone, a blister or a burn from hot sand. Design something that helps them find a hurt before it gets worse.
constraints: It must work every day without anyone feeling pain.
It must be cheap and easy to make in an Indian home.
It must be safe and gentle on the skin.
materials: cardboard, cloth, cotton wool and cello tape
old chappals or slippers to look at
general: A daily foot check with a mirror, morning and night, looking for red marks, cuts and blisters.
Soft, closed shoes that are checked inside for stones before putting them on.
Testing bath water with an elbow, which can still feel heat, before stepping in.
creative: A chappal with a bright white lining, so a drop of blood or a wet blister shows at once.
A family checklist chart on the bathroom door, ticked every evening.
A small cloth-covered tray by the door to tip out each shoe before wearing it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own foot guard. Draw it, label each part, and say which danger it catches.

flow.do: Read the problem together. List the dangers for a foot that cannot feel pain.
flow.say: Pain usually tells us when something is wrong. If someone cannot feel it, what could hurt their feet without them knowing?
flow.kid: Imagine your feet cannot feel pain. What could hurt them?
flow.context: This is an engineering challenge. You design a way to protect feet that cannot feel pain, as doctors in Vellore did.

flow.do: Draw two ideas, choose one, and make a model or a chart.
flow.say: Draw two ideas. Which one would catch more dangers? Let's make that one.
flow.kid: Draw two ideas. Pick the best one. Make it.

flow.do: Test the idea: hide a small pebble in a shoe, and see if the design finds it.
flow.say: Let's test it. I hid a pebble in this shoe. Does your design find it?
flow.kid: A pebble is hiding in a shoe. Does your design find it?

challenges.title: Build a Prawn's Balance Pit: a tilt detector
challenges.problem: A prawn knows which way is down because sand grains roll and press on sensing hairs in a small pit. Build a tilt detector that shows which way it is tipped, using something that rolls.
constraints: It must show at least four directions: forward, back, left and right.
It must use only things from home.
You must be able to tell the direction with your eyes shut, by sound or touch.
materials: a small round steel box or a plastic lid
a marble, a bead or a dried chana
small bells, or bits of foil, or four small heaps of different things
general: Put a marble in a round lid. Tape a different texture to each side. With eyes shut, feel which side the marble has rolled to.
Hang four small bells round the inside edge of a box, so the rolling bead rings the bell on the low side.
creative: Use four different sounds on four sides, so you know the direction by ear.
Use a few grains of rice instead of one marble, like the prawn's sand grains.
Make two detectors, one for each side, like a prawn's two pits.
challenges.your_turn: Now build your own tilt detector. Test it with your eyes shut, and explain how it is like a prawn's balance pit and like your ear crystals.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Talk about how the prawn's sand works.
flow.say: In the prawn's pit, the sand rolls to the low side and presses on hairs. How could a marble in a box tell us which way it is tipped?
flow.kid: Sand rolls to the low side. How can a marble show which way is down?
flow.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a tilt detector that works like a prawn's balance pit.

flow.do: Draw an idea, then build it.
flow.say: Draw your detector first. What will tell you which side is low?
flow.kid: Draw your idea. Then build it.

flow.do: Test it: your child shuts their eyes while you tip the detector. Can they tell the direction?
flow.say: Eyes shut. I will tip it. Which way is it tipped?
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. A grown-up tips it. Which way?
