quiz.p: Which of these is a sense that is NOT on the list of five?
quiz.why: Balance has its own organs in the inner ear. Sight, taste and hearing are on the old list of five. Many more senses exist, such as body position, warmth, cold and pain.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, spins round 10 times and sits down. The room seems to keep turning. What is really still moving?
opts: The liquid in the loops of her inner ear
quiz.why: The liquid in her semicircular canals keeps swirling after she stops, so her brain thinks she is still turning. Her eyes do flick for a moment, but because the brain thinks the head is turning, not by themselves.

quiz.p: A steel plate and a wooden board have been in the same room all day. Which is true?
opts: They are at the same temperature, but the steel feels colder
They are at the same temperature, and they feel the same
quiz.why: Things left in one room all reach room temperature. The steel feels colder because it carries heat away from your skin faster. Picking 'the steel is colder' is the most common answer, but the ice test shows it is not.

quiz.p: In the Ice Race, Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, puts one ice cube on a steel plate and one on a wooden board. Which melts first?
opts: The one on the wooden board
The one on the steel plate
Neither, because the steel keeps it frozen
quiz.why: Steel carries heat from the room into the ice quickly, so that cube melts first. Wood carries heat slowly. If the steel were really colder, its ice would last longer.

quiz.p: You scratch your ear in the dark. How does your hand find your ear?
opts: Your hand can see in the dark
Stretch sensors in your muscles and joints tell your brain where your hand is
quiz.why: This sense is called proprioception. The stretch sensors send signals all the time, so your brain knows where every part of you is, without your eyes.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy helping make dosas, touches a hot tawa and his hand jumps back before he even says 'ouch'. What is this quick movement called?
quiz.why: A reflex is a quick movement your body makes without you choosing it. The signal goes to the spinal cord and straight back to the arm muscles, so it is faster than thinking.

quiz.p: Doctors in Vellore found why people with leprosy lost parts of their fingers. What was the main reason?
opts: The disease ate the fingers away
Their nerves stopped carrying pain, so they got hurt without noticing
They did not wash their hands
quiz.why: Paul Brand showed that the flesh was healthy. Without pain, people kept using burnt or cut hands, and the wounds got worse. Daily checks and soft shoes protected them.

quiz.p: A sardine is a small sea fish. She swims in a dark sea in a big shoal. How does she turn with the others without bumping?
opts: Her lateral line feels the water move as they turn
quiz.why: The lateral line is a row of sensors along each side of a fish. It feels the water push as nearby fish move, so the shoal can turn together, even in the dark.

quiz.p: A prawn has just moulted, wriggling out of their old shell. Why do they pick up grains of sand?
opts: To put them in the balance pits at the base of their short feelers
quiz.why: The balance pits are part of the shell, so the old sand goes away with it. New sand grains rest on the sensing hairs and show the prawn which way is down.

quiz.p: After chewing pudina, Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3, sips water and it feels very cold. Why?
opts: Menthol in pudina switches on her cold receptors
The water came from the fridge
quiz.why: Menthol switches on cold receptors, so they send 'cold' signals though the water's temperature has not changed.

quiz.p: Riya, a girl in Class 4, wants to test if she gets dizzier after 10 spins than after 5. What makes it a fair test?
opts: Spin at the same speed and rest until normal between tries
Do 5 spins on the bed and 10 on the floor
quiz.why: In a fair test, only the number of spins changes. The speed, the place and the rest between tries stay the same, so any difference comes from the number of spins.

quiz.p: Why do many children feel sick reading a book in a moving car?
opts: Their ears feel the car moving, but their eyes, on the book, see no movement
quiz.why: The best-known idea is that the balance sense and the eyes disagree. Scientists still argue about it. Looking out at the road usually helps.

items.p: Match each sense to what it tells you.
pairs: when your head turns or tilts
where your hands and feet are
that something is hurting your body
hunger, thirst and needing the toilet
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five senses are not on the list of five, and each has its own receptors.

items.p: The three tiny loops of liquid in each inner ear are called the semicircular ____.
items.why: The semicircular canals feel the head turning, because the liquid inside lags behind and bends tiny hairs.

items.p: Two things left in the same room all day are at the same temperature, even if one feels colder.
items.why: True. Both reach room temperature. A good conductor of heat, such as steel, feels colder because it takes heat from your skin faster.

items.p: Which of these is the best conductor of heat?
items.why: Metals such as steel carry heat quickly. Cloth, wood and plastic carry heat slowly, so they are poor conductors.

items.p: Sort these moments by the sense that noticed them.
items: feeling the lift start
Balance
touching your nose with eyes shut
Body position
cold tiles under bare feet
Warm and cold
a thorn in your finger
Pain
the room spinning after a swing
Balance
eating without looking at your hand
Body position
items.a: see items
items.why: Each moment uses a different hidden sense. Balance feels turning and speeding up. Body position feels where your parts are.

items.p: In the Ice Race, the steel felt colder, but its ice melted first. Explain why, using the words 'heat' and 'conductor'.
items.a: Steel is a good conductor of heat. It carries heat away from my warm hand fast, so it feels cold. It also carries heat from the room into the ice fast, so the ice melts first. Wood is a poor conductor, so it does both slowly.
items.why: A strong answer explains both results with the same idea: steel moves heat quickly, in both directions.

items.p: Draw the bowl of water from Spin and Stop, just after the bowl stopped. Show with arrows what the water was doing.
items.a: A still bowl, with curved arrows showing the water and the paper arrow still turning.
items.why: The water keeps turning after the bowl stops, just as the liquid in your ear loops keeps swirling after you stop spinning.

items.p: Why can you still walk down the stairs in a power cut?
opts: Your eyes work in the dark
Your balance and body-position senses keep working without light
items.why: The balance organs and the stretch sensors in your muscles need no light. They tell you where your feet are and whether you are tipping.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Stretch sensors in muscles, ear crystals, semicircular canals, taste buds.
items.a: taste buds
items.why: Taste buds are part of taste, one of the old five senses. The others are parts of the balance sense or the body-position sense.

items.p: Pain is always bad for the body.
items.why: False. Short, sharp pain warns you to stop doing something harmful. People who cannot feel pain get hurt much more often.

items.p: Label the parts of the inner ear on the drawing: semicircular canals, the pouch with ear crystals, the nerve to the brain.
items.why: The canals feel turning, the crystals feel tilting and speeding up, and the nerve carries both signals to the brain.
items.art: A simple drawing of the inner ear: three loops at the top, a small pouch below them, and a thick line leading away, with three blank label lines.

items.p: Put these in order: what happens when you touch a hot tawa?
items: your hand jerks away
pain receptors in your fingertip fire
the signal reaches your spinal cord
you feel the pain and say 'ouch'
a: pain receptors in your fingertip fire
the signal reaches your spinal cord
you feel the pain and say 'ouch'
items.why: The reflex goes from the spinal cord straight back to the muscles, so the hand often moves before the brain feels the pain.

items.p: The sense of where your body parts are is called ____.
items.why: Proprioception comes from stretch sensors in muscles, tendons and joints.

items.p: Name one animal with a sense people do not have. What problem does the animal have, and how does the sense help?
items.a: A prawn lives in dark, moving water and needs to know which way is up. Sand grains in their balance pits roll to the low side and press on hairs, so the prawn knows which way is down.
items.why: A strong answer says the animal's own problem first, then how the sense solves it.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, and her brother Karthik touch the steel railing and the wooden door on their balcony in the morning.

views.says: The railing is colder than the door. I can feel it.
They are the same temperature. The railing just takes heat from your hand faster.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the Ice Race. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Divya, using the evidence that ice melts faster on steel, which could not happen if the steel were colder. It also says Karthik is right about what he feels: the railing really does feel colder.
items.why: Both are partly right. The feeling is real, but it measures heat leaving the hand, not temperature.

items.p: A lift starts going up, and you feel heavier for a moment. Then it moves smoothly, and you feel normal. Explain why, using the ear crystals.
items.a: When the lift speeds up, the crystals lag behind and press down harder on the hairs, so I feel heavier. At a steady speed nothing presses extra, so I feel normal. My balance sense feels changes in speed, not steady movement.
items.why: A strong answer explains that the crystals respond to speeding up and slowing down, not to steady movement.

items.p: Kathak dancers spin many times without falling. What do they do with their eyes and head?
opts: Fix their eyes on one spot and turn the head quickly at the end of each spin
items.why: Fixing the eyes on one spot, called spotting, keeps the head still for most of each turn. The ear loops get less steady spinning, so the dancer gets less dizzy.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, did Find the Dot. His pencil landed 2 cm from the dot with his eyes shut, but right on it with his eyes open. What does this tell you about how the senses work together?
items.a: His body-position sense got his hand close, but his eyes made the last correction. Senses check each other, and with both, the hand is more exact.
items.why: A strong answer says each sense does part of the job, and the brain puts them together.

items.p: On a hot afternoon, a steel railing in the sun feels hotter than a wooden door in the sun. Why?
opts: Steel carries heat into your skin faster than wood
The sun shines more on steel
items.why: If something is warmer than your skin, steel carries its heat into your skin fast, so it feels hotter. It is the same idea as the Ice Race, the other way round.

items.p: You feel the steady part of a smooth lift ride just as strongly as the start.
items.why: False. The balance sense feels changes: starting, stopping and turning. At a steady speed, you feel nothing extra.

items.p: Draw two hands: one on a steel plate and one on a wooden board. Use arrows to show the heat leaving each hand. Make the arrows bigger where more heat leaves.
items.a: Big arrows from the hand into the steel, small arrows from the hand into the wood.
items.why: More heat leaves the skin into the steel, so that hand cools faster and feels colder.

items.p: Match each animal to their problem.
pairs: finding a warm rat in the dark
knowing where an insect hit the web
finding someone to bite for blood for her eggs
turning with the shoal without bumping
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The python uses heat pits, the spider feels web shakes with her legs, the mosquito senses breath, and the sardine uses the lateral line.

items.p: The chemical in mint that switches on cold receptors is called ____.
items.why: Menthol switches on the same receptors that fire when something cold touches you. It does not change the temperature.

items.p: Sneha, a girl in Class 4, feels sick reading in the car on the ghat road to Munnar. Her grandmother and her cousin give advice.

views.says: Your ears and eyes are telling you different things. Look out of the front window at the road.
Your body cannot keep steady on the bends. Sit in the middle where the ride is smoothest and lean back on the seat.

items.ask: Whose idea fits what you know about the balance sense? Give your reason. Then say what is good about the other idea.
items.a: A strong answer explains the eyes-and-ears idea with the balance organs, and says the other idea is also studied by scientists. Both pieces of advice help, so trying both is sensible.
items.why: Scientists still argue about the cause of car sickness, so a good answer weighs both ideas.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A steel tumbler, an aluminium lid, a copper vessel, a cotton napkin.
items.a: a cotton napkin
items.why: Cotton is a poor conductor of heat. The others are metals and good conductors, so they feel colder to the touch.

items.p: Your leg 'falls asleep' after sitting cross-legged, and you wobble when you stand up. Which sense is not working properly, and why do you wobble?
items.a: My body-position sense. The squeezed nerves stop sending signals from my leg for a while, so my brain does not know where my foot is, and I cannot balance on it.
items.why: A strong answer links the missing signals to the wobble.

items.p: Why is a short, sharp pain useful?
opts: It makes you stop and protect the hurt part
items.why: Pain warns you, so you pull away, rest or look after the hurt part before more damage is done.

items.p: Sort these: does each one feel colder or warmer than you would expect, and why?
items: a steel spoon in a cool room
Feels colder
a cotton mat on a cold floor
Feels warmer
the air after chewing mint
Feels colder
a mouthful of green chilli
Feels warmer
items.a: see items
items.why: Steel takes heat fast, and mint fools the cold receptors. Cotton takes heat slowly, and chilli fools the heat receptors.

items.p: Label the senses on the drawing of a girl climbing stairs: balance in her ears, body position in her legs, touch in her hand on the rail.
items.why: Climbing stairs uses several senses together. The brain puts them into one picture.
items.art: A girl climbing stairs holding a rail, with three blank label lines pointing to her ear, her leg and her hand.

items.p: In the Dizzy Timer, Kavya, a girl in Class 3, felt dizzy for 6 seconds after 5 spins and 14 seconds after 10 spins. Explain the difference.
items.a: After 10 spins, the liquid in her ear loops was swirling more, so it took longer to slow down and stop. While it swirled, her brain thought she was still turning.
items.why: A strong answer links the number of spins to how much the liquid was moving.

items.p: Many people think metal is colder than wood. Design a test, different from the Ice Race, to show whether they are right.
items.a: Leave a steel tumbler and a wooden cup in the same room. Put a thermometer against each and wait. Both show the same reading. Or put a dab of butter on each in a warm room and see which melts first.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing, uses a measurement or a result that does not depend on the hand, and says what each result would mean.

items.p: Scientists still count the senses differently.

views.who: Dr. Anjali, a scientist who counts receptors
views.says: Warmth and cold have different receptors in different spots, so they are two senses.

views.who: Dr. Ravi, a scientist who counts experiences
views.says: Warmth and cold both feel like temperature, so they are one sense.

items.ask: Which way of counting makes more sense to you? Use the Cold Spot Map as evidence. Then say one good point the other scientist makes.
items.a: A strong answer uses the map, which showed separate cold spots, to support counting receptors, or argues that what matters is how it feels. It names one strength of the other view.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The number of senses depends on how you choose to count.

items.p: In 1893, Alois Kreidl gave freshly moulted shrimps iron filings instead of sand, and held a magnet above them. Predict what the shrimps did, and explain why.
items.a: The shrimps tipped over. The magnet attracted the iron in their balance pits, so the iron pressed on the hairs as if down had moved. The shrimps turned their bodies to match the new 'down'.
items.why: A strong answer explains that the shrimp feels which way the grains press, and the magnet changed that.

items.p: Astronauts in space often feel sick for the first few days. Which is the best explanation?
opts: With almost no feeling of down, their ear crystals send strange signals that do not match their eyes
items.why: In orbit, the ear crystals no longer rest towards one side, so the balance sense and the eyes disagree. Most astronauts get used to it within a few days.

items.p: A child is born unable to feel pain. Write three rules the family could follow to keep the child safe.
items.a: Check the child's skin, hands and feet every day for cuts, burns and bruises. Test bath water and food temperature for them. Teach them to look carefully at what they touch and to rest a hurt part even when it does not hurt.
items.why: A strong answer replaces each job pain does with a check the family can do.

items.p: In the Ice Race, Ammu, a girl in Class 3, found her two cubes melted at almost the same time. Which is the most likely reason?
opts: The steel plate had just come out of a hot sink, or the board was in the sun
items.why: If the two surfaces did not start at the same temperature, the test is not fair. Leaving both in the same shady spot for an hour fixes it. A thicker metal, such as an aluminium lid, gives a bigger difference.

items.p: Draw a cartoon strip of four pictures showing how a fish's lateral line helps them escape a hunter in muddy water.
items.a: 1. A fish in muddy water. 2. A bigger fish coming from behind, out of sight. 3. Water pushed ahead of the hunter reaching the fish's side. 4. The fish darting away.
items.why: A strong strip shows the fish's problem, the water movement, the sense, and the escape, in order.

items.p: A thermometer and your hand measure the same thing.
items.why: False. A thermometer measures temperature. Your hand feels how fast heat moves in or out of the skin, which also depends on what the thing is made of.

items.p: Your hand jerks away from a hot tawa before you feel the pain. Why is it useful that the reflex does not wait for the brain?
items.a: The signal only has to go to the spinal cord and back, which is quicker. Every bit of time the hand stays on the tawa burns it more, so moving first saves skin.
items.why: A strong answer links speed to less damage.

items.p: Put these in order: what happens in your ear when you start spinning, keep spinning, and stop?
items: the liquid catches up and turns with you
the liquid lags behind and bends the hairs one way
the liquid keeps swirling and bends the hairs the other way
the liquid slows and stops, and the dizziness ends
a: the liquid lags behind and bends the hairs one way
the liquid catches up and turns with you
the liquid keeps swirling and bends the hairs the other way
the liquid slows and stops, and the dizziness ends
items.why: This is why you feel turning at the start, little while spinning steadily, and turning the other way after you stop.

items.p: Match each test to the sense it tested.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each test in this unit picked out one hidden sense.

items.p: Some people say a sense is 'a window onto the world'. After the Ice Race, would you agree? What does your sense of cold really show you?
items.a: Partly. The sense of cold does tell me about the world, but not the temperature. It shows how fast heat is leaving my hand, which depends on me and on what I touch.
items.why: A strong answer uses the Ice Race to say what the sense actually reports.

People have it

items.why: People share many senses with other animals, but fish, pythons and prawns have some we lack.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? The lateral line of a fish, the whiskers of a cat, the eyes of an owl, the heat pits of a python.
items.a: the eyes of an owl
items.why: Owls' eyes are very good, but people have eyes too. The others sense things people cannot: water flow, air movement through whiskers, and the heat of a body in the dark.

items.p: Make up a new test of a hidden sense that nobody in this unit has done. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same, and what you would measure.
items.a: For example: does standing on one foot get easier after a week of practice? Change the day, keep the same foot, the same floor and eyes open, and measure seconds with a stopwatch.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing, keeps the rest the same, and measures a number.

applications: Doctors test the balance sense by watching a patient's eyes after they turn their head, or after warm or cool water is put gently in the ear.
Pilots train in spinning chairs to learn that their balance sense can fool them in cloud, so they trust their instruments.
Cooking vessels have wooden or plastic handles, because these carry heat slowly and do not burn the hand.
Mint and menthol are used in toothpaste, sweets and balms to make the mouth or skin feel cool.
People with diabetes or leprosy check their feet every day, because they may not feel a wound.
Engineers have built robot boats and underwater robots with flow sensors that copy a fish's lateral line.
Physiotherapists help people recover their body-position sense after an injury, with balance boards and eyes-shut exercises.
Mosquito traps use carbon dioxide and warmth to attract mosquitoes, copying the signals they follow to find people.

open_questions.q: How do signals from cold receptors become the feeling of cold?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can follow the signals into the brain, but nobody knows how signals become a feeling.

open_questions.q: Exactly why do some people get car sick or seasick, and others never do?
open_questions.why_open: There are several ideas, such as the senses disagreeing or the body struggling to stay steady. None of them explains every case.

open_questions.q: How many senses do people really have?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how you count, by receptor or by experience. Scientists have not agreed on one way.

open_questions.q: Do elephants hear through their feet?
open_questions.why_open: Elephants make very low rumbles that travel through the ground. Some studies, such as Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell's, found that elephants react to these ground rumbles. How far and how well they use them is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the Dizzy Timer, Kavya felt dizzy for 6 seconds after 5 turns and 14 seconds after 10 turns. How many more seconds did 10 turns give? If the pattern goes on, guess how long 15 turns would give, and say why it is only a guess.
maths.answer: 8 more seconds. A guess for 15 turns is about 22 seconds, but it is only a guess.
maths.explain: 14 - 6 = 8. Each extra 5 turns added 8 seconds, so 14 + 8 = 22. It is only a guess, because the liquid in the ear may stop speeding up after a while, and we have not tested 15 turns.
maths.context: This is about the Dizzy Timer, where you spin and time how long the dizziness lasts.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a pattern lets you make a prediction, and the maths also shows why you must test a guess before trusting it.

maths.problem: In Find the Dot, Arjun's misses with his writing hand were 2, 1, 3, 1 and 2 cm. With his other hand they were 4, 3, 2, 3 and 3 cm. Which hand did better? By how much in total?
maths.answer: His writing hand did better, by 6 cm in total.
maths.explain: Writing hand: 2 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 9 cm. Other hand: 4 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 15 cm. 15 - 9 = 6. A smaller total miss means the hand landed closer.
maths.context: This is about Find the Dot, where you try to touch a dot with your eyes shut and measure each miss.
maths.why_maths: Adding up all five misses is fairer than looking at one try, because one try can be luck.

maths.problem: In the Ice Race, the cube on the steel plate melted in 15 minutes. The cube on the wooden board took 45 minutes. How many times as long did the wooden board's cube last?
maths.explain: 45 divided by 15 is 3. So the cube on the wood lasted 3 times as long as the cube on the steel. These are made-up numbers, and your own times will depend on the room.
maths.context: This is about the Ice Race, where you put one ice cube on a steel plate and one on a wooden board.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'three times as long' compares the two surfaces in a way that still makes sense in a warmer or cooler room.

maths.problem: On her Cold Spot Map, Lakshmi tested 16 squares. 10 felt cold and the rest felt only like a touch. How many felt only like a touch? What fraction of the squares felt cold?
maths.answer: 6 felt only like a touch. 10 out of 16 felt cold, which is the same as 5 out of 8.
maths.explain: 16 - 10 = 6. 10 sixteenths is the same as 5 eighths, because both numbers can be halved.
maths.context: This is about the Cold Spot Map, where you touch each square of a grid on your hand with a cold key.
maths.why_maths: A fraction lets you compare your map with a friend's, even if they tested a different number of squares.

maths.problem: Meenakshi's diary had 4 balance messages, 7 body-position messages, 5 warm-and-cold messages, 2 pain messages and 12 inside-sense messages in 5 days. Draw a bar chart. Which sense sent the most messages? Why do you think so?
maths.answer: The inside senses sent the most, 12 messages.
maths.explain: The tallest bar is inside senses, 12. That makes sense: every day she felt hungry, thirsty and needed the toilet several times, but she rarely got hurt.
maths.context: This is about My Body Messages Diary, where you write down the messages your hidden senses send for five days.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which senses were busiest, and then you can ask why.

roots.context: We have tested our balance, our body sense, warmth, cold and pain. Now we ask what these senses tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The steel plate felt colder than the wooden board, though both sat in one room all morning. Yet the ice melted faster on the steel. Steel carries heat fast, out of your hand and into the ice. So your skin feels heat moving in or out, not how hot a thing is.
deep_truth.habit: We think our hand reads temperature like a thermometer, so whatever feels colder must be colder. But the skin reports the flow of heat through it. Two things at the same temperature can feel very different.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Ice Race, the steel plate felt colder to the touch. The ice cube on the steel melted much faster than the one on the wooden board. Both had been in the same room for at least an hour, so both were at room temperature.

three.who_am_i: You are always trading heat with everything you touch, and your skin keeps track of every trade.
three.what_is_life: A prawn uses sand from the sea floor to find down, and you use crystals your body made. Every living being builds senses for the life they live.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of things that mosquitoes, fish and spiders sense and we cannot. What we feel is only part of what is there.

roots.thread: Heat flows from warmer things to cooler things everywhere: from the Sun to the Earth, from hot tea to the air, from your hand to a plate. Your skin does not stand outside that flow. It is one of the places the flow passes through, and the feeling of cold is that flow passing. The same flow melted the ice. So your feeling and the melting ice were two signs of one movement of heat.

teachings.teaching: Krishna tells Arjuna that the touch of the senses with things brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These come and go, and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them steadily.
teachings.link: The Gita calls cold and heat a meeting of the senses with things. Your test found the same. The cold was in the meeting, as heat moved between your hand and the steel, and it changed when the meeting changed.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha teaches that when walking, one knows 'I am walking'. When standing, sitting or lying down, one knows that too. One stays aware of the body as it moves.
teachings.link: Knowing how your body is placed, without looking, is the sense of body position. The Buddha asked people to notice this sense, which works quietly all day.

science.text: Heat always flows from a warmer thing to a cooler thing, and it flows faster through metals than through wood, cloth or air.
Separate receptors in the skin detect cooling and warming. Some of them were found only in the last 30 years, and the work won the 2021 Nobel Prize.
How signals from cold receptors become the feeling of cold is not known.

other_view.view: Cold is just the name we give to signals from cold receptors. Saying the feeling is a meeting with the world adds nothing to the science of how heat flows and how nerves fire.

practice.title: Feel the heat moving
practice.say: Close your eyes. Rest one palm on a steel tumbler and the other on a wooden spoon or a cloth. Keep them still for one minute. Notice how the cold under the steel fades. Your skin is giving its warmth to the steel, and the steel is getting warmer. Now lift both hands, and breathe slowly three times. Can you still feel where the steel was?
practice.kid: Shut your eyes. One hand on a steel tumbler. One hand on a cloth. Keep still for one minute. Does the cold fade? Your warmth is going into the steel.

ask: If your skin feels heat moving, not temperature, what else might your senses be telling you that is different from what you think?
The steel took your warmth until it was nearly as warm as you. Where does your warmth go when you touch things all day?
A prawn uses sand from outside their body to sense. Can something from outside you become part of how you sense?

playtest: Every activity was walked through as if in a city flat. The Ice Race uses a steel thali and a wooden or plastic chopping board, which most kitchens have. A thin steel thali gives a smaller difference than a thick metal block, so the steps add an aluminium lid as a third surface and say to leave both surfaces in the shade for an hour first. In a warm room the cube on steel is mostly gone in 10 to 15 minutes. Spinning is done slowly on a mat with a grown-up close, and children who feel sick easily can time a grown-up instead. The bowl model needs a round steel bowl on a plate so it turns smoothly. The Cold Spot Map may show every square as cold if the tip is too wide, so the step suggests an opened paper clip. Mint leaves can be replaced by a mint sweet. The project and games need only paper. No purchases are needed. The spine is the spinning hook, Spin and Stop, the Ice Race, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: For thousands of years, people believed leprosy made fingers and toes rot and fall off by itself. People with leprosy lost parts of their hands and feet, and many were pushed out of their towns. In the late 1940s, Paul Brand, a British surgeon at the Christian Medical College in Vellore, began to look closely. He noticed that his patients often hurt their hands while working, and did not seem to notice. He tested the hands of many patients. Their flesh was healthy, but the nerves had stopped carrying pain. So their hands were being hurt in daily life. A patient could hold a hot cooking pot, walk all day with a sharp stone in a shoe, or keep using a cut hand, and never feel it. The wounds got worse because nobody rested them. His wife, Margaret Brand, an eye doctor, found that the same thing harmed the eyes. Patients who could not feel their eyes did not blink enough to protect them. With soft shoes, careful habits and checking hands and feet every day, people with leprosy kept their fingers and toes. Leprosy can now be cured with medicines that are free in India.
how_we_found_out.who: Paul Brand, a surgeon, and Margaret Brand, an eye doctor, at the Christian Medical College, Vellore
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the disease itself ate away fingers and toes. Paul Brand showed that leprosy damages the nerves, so people stop feeling pain, and the injuries come from everyday use that nobody feels.
